summary: This informational memo discusses vendor extensions to PPP, the Point-to-Point Protocol, which carries multi-protocol datagrams over point-to-point links using LCP and NCPs. It provides information for the community and is not a standard.

eli5.summary: Room in a standard letter format where companies can add their own special notes.

questions: what is the ppp vendor specific packet
what is an oui in ppp
what is the cf0000 oui series
subtitle: A standard slot in PPP's control packets and options where vendors can put private extensions without asking IANA for numbers.

tldr.problem: Some PPP implementors do not want to publish their proprietary algorithms and attributes, and secretly self-assigned Code and Type numbers risk clashing with each other.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2153 defines a Vendor Specific packet (Code 0) and a Vendor-Specific configuration option (Type 0). Both carry a three-octet OUI naming the vendor, a one-octet Kind and vendor-defined data.
tldr.outcome: Vendors get a general feature of all PPP control protocols without requesting proprietary numbers from IANA. The memo is Informational and has since been updated by RFC 5342 and RFC 7042.

today: RFC 2153 is Informational and updates RFC 1661 and RFC 1962. It has itself been updated by RFC 5342 and RFC 7042.

sections.title: Why Vendors Need a Reserved Slot
sections.content:
The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) has an extensible Link Control Protocol (LCP) and a family of Network Control Protocols (NCPs). RFC 1661 defines the packet format and basic facilities. Packets carry a Code field and configuration options carry a Type field, and the values are listed in the "Assigned Numbers" document.

Some implementors might not need or want to publish their proprietary algorithms and attributes. RFC 2153 gives them a way to specify these without encumbering the IANA with proprietary number requests.

The RFC states its rationale: it is defined as a general feature of all PPP control protocols, to avoid future conflicts in vendor secretly self-assigned Code and Type numbers.
sections.eli5: Companies sometimes want to keep their special ideas private. Instead of each one grabbing a made-up number and maybe clashing, everyone gets one shared place to put private things.

sections.title: The Vendor Specific Packet
sections.content:
A Vendor Specific packet is an LCP or NCP packet with the Code field set to 0. The sender also sets the Identifier, inserts its local Magic-Number (if any), and fills in the OUI and Kind fields. The Value(s) field holds any desired data, but must not exceed the default MRU minus twelve.

The Length is at least 12; when it is exactly twelve, no Value(s) field is present. The Identifier MUST be changed for each Vendor Specific packet sent. Until the Magic-Number option has been successfully negotiated, the Magic-Number MUST be sent as zero.

These packets MAY be sent at any time, including before LCP has reached the Opened state. Receiving one causes the RXR or RUC event, and the response is vendor specific. Receipt of a Code-Reject for the packet SHOULD generate the RXJ+ (permitted) event.
sections.eli5: It is a message with a special label that says 'this part belongs to one company'. What happens next is up to that company, and if the other side does not understand it, that is fine.

sections.title: The Vendor-Specific Configuration Option
sections.content:
The same idea applies to option negotiation. The Vendor-Specific option uses Type 0 in the LCP configuration option format. Its Length is at least 6, and when it is exactly six there is no Value(s) field.

Before accepting the option, an implementation must verify that the OUI and Kind specify a known mechanism, and that any vendor specific negotiation values are fully understood.

The Kind field is one octet that gives a sub-type for the OUI. It is not standardized; each OUI implements its own values, and the vendor may extend Kind to include zero or more octets of the Value(s) field.
sections.eli5: When two sides agree on settings, a company can also offer a private setting. You only say yes if you really know what that company's setting means.

sections.title: Organizationally Unique Identifiers
sections.content:
The three-octet Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI) names the organization that administers the meaning of the message. It is based on IEEE 802 vendor assignments. Vendors that want to use their IEEE 802 OUI should also register it with IANA.

A vendor without an IEEE-assigned OUI can instead request a PPP specific OUI from IANA, assigned from the CF0000 series. In that series the two least significant bits of the most significant octet (the locally-assigned and broadcast/multicast bits) are both set to 1.

The RFC explains that this is for vendors that cannot use IEEE assignments, such as software-only vendors. Multicast has no meaning in PPP, so an IEEE-assigned OUI would have the multicast bit cleared to 0. The CF0000 series was arbitrarily chosen to match the PPP NLPID CF, as a mnemonic convenience.
sections.eli5: The OUI is a company's name tag. Companies with an official tag use it; those without can ask for a special PPP tag that starts with the same marker.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's security section is a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this document. Nothing in the text says how a receiver should authenticate the vendor behind an OUI, so the meaning and safety of the extension data is left to each vendor's own mechanism.
sections.eli5: The memo does not say anything about safety, so each company has to look after that itself.

fields.name: Identifier
fields.desc: Changed for each Vendor Specific packet sent.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: At least 12; no Value(s) field when exactly 12.

fields.name: Magic-Number
fields.desc: Transmitted as zero until the Magic-Number option is negotiated.

fields.name: Kind
fields.desc: Sub-type for the OUI; each OUI defines its own values.
